t.1.120.1: Janamejaya said: O great brahmin, you should also tell of the birth of Kṛpa. How was he born from a clump of reeds, and how did he obtain his weapons?
t.1.120.2: The great seer Gautama had a son, O great king, known by the name of Śaradvān, who, it is said, was born together with arrows, O mighty one.
t.1.120.3: His mind did not turn to the study of the Vedas so much as it turned to the science of archery, O scorcher of foes.
t.1.120.4: Just as the expounders of the Veda attained the Vedas through austerity, so he, endowed with austerity, obtained all the weapons.
t.1.120.5: Through his utter devotion to the science of archery and through his vast austerity, that Gautama greatly troubled the king of the gods.
t.1.120.7: Having approached the lovely hermitage of Śaradvat, the young maiden enticed Gautama, who was bearing his bow and arrows.
t.1.120.6: Then the lord of the gods sent forth a divine maiden named Jālapadī, saying, “Create an obstacle to his austerities,” O Kaurava.
t.1.120.8: Seeing in the forest that Apsaras clad in a single garment, whose form was unequalled in the world, Gautama stood with eyes wide open.
t.1.120.9: His bow and arrows fell from his hands to the ground, and on seeing her a trembling arose in his body.
t.1.120.10: But he, the greatly wise one, owing to the greatness of his knowledge and his possession of austerity, held himself steady with supreme fortitude.
t.1.120.11: But, O king, because of the agitation that suddenly came over him, his semen flowed forth, and he did not even notice it.
t.1.120.12: Leaving behind both that hermitage and that apsaras, the sage departed; and that semen of his fell upon a clump of reeds.
t.1.120.14: While King Śaṃtanu was out hunting, a certain soldier of his army happened by chance to see that pair of twins in the forest.
t.1.120.13: And having fallen upon a clump of reeds, it split in two, O king; then a pair of twins was born to him, Gautama Śaradvat.
t.1.120.16: Then the king, filled with compassion, took up that pair of twins and went straight home, saying, "These two are my children."
t.1.120.15: Seeing the bow with its arrow and the black antelope skins, he concluded that the pair was the offspring of a brahmin who had mastered the science of archery. Then he showed the twins, together with the arrow, to the king.
t.1.120.17: Then he raised them and furnished them with the sacraments. Gautama, too, having then gone away, devoted himself wholly to the science of archery.
t.1.120.18: "Since these two children have been raised by me out of compassion," so thinking, the lord of the earth therefore gave them that very name.
t.1.120.21: Then all those great chariot-warriors mastered the science of archery: the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the mighty Pāṇḍavas, the Vṛṣṇis, and other kings who had gathered from various lands.
t.1.120.19: Through his ascetic power Gautama discovered the two who had been placed there, and having come, he then told him everything, their lineage and the rest.
t.1.120.20: Then he taught him in full the fourfold science of archery and the various weapons, all of that secret lore; and in a very short time he attained the rank of a supreme teacher.
